title: Space Age Rationalism

design.artifact: Ball Chair: sketched January 1963, shown at the Cologne furniture fair in 1966

layers.tension: The space race and faith in technical progress: the future is designed like a mass-produced product, clean and optimistic.
layers.material: Fibreglass and resin, vinyl, stiff fabrics and PVC. Smooth, white, industrial surfaces with no trace of the hand.
layers.artifacts: Short A-line dress and white boots by Courrèges. Eero Aarnio's Ball Chair: a hollow sphere the body steps into and withdraws inside.
layers.gesture: The body is freed and geometric: bare legs, a quick stride. The seat wraps around its occupant and separates them from the space outside.
layers.decomposition: The white yellows and the fibreglass cracks. The clean utopia survives as a retro-futurist quotation, nostalgia for a future that never came.

to_verify: Dates checked against sources. Still to decide: the link with the space race. Aarnio himself says it was not intended and that the timing with Gagarin's flight was a coincidence.

sources.label: Journal of Antiques · Courrèges, Space Age

title: Plastic Pop & Metal Couture

fashion.artifact: '12 Unwearable Dresses in Contemporary Materials', Paris, 1966

design.artifact: Panton Chair: shown in 1967, serial production with Vitra from 1968

layers.tension: The space race and faith in synthetic materials: the body and the home become surfaces of the same industry.
layers.material: Rhodoid discs and metal rings, plastic and wire with no fabric. Fibreglass-reinforced polyester, then moulded polyurethane foam.
layers.artifacts: Rabanne's dresses in plastic and rings, assembled like mail. The Panton Chair: a chair in a single piece, with no legs.
layers.gesture: The body is assembled rather than dressed. The chair is sat in as one continuous curve, with no joints.
layers.decomposition: The plastic that promised a future does not hold: Panton production stops in 1979 because polystyrene is not durable enough, and the material has to be reformulated several times.

to_verify: The Museum at FIT dates the wedding dress to 1968 but shows it in Vogue, June 1966: choose which piece to show. Add a source for the phrase 'Rhodoid and rings' (the FIT source says plastic and metal rings).

sources.label: The Museum at FIT · Rabanne wedding dress

title: Industrial Punk & Radical Design

fashion.artifact: Shop at 430 King's Road: SEX (1974–76), then Seditionaries (1976–79)

layers.tension: Economic crisis and distrust of institutions. Clothing and architecture become a gesture against good taste and against the idea of linear progress.
layers.material: Rubber, leather, zips, chains and safety pins. In Superstudio's projects, the grid and laminate: industrial materials used as provocation.
layers.artifacts: Garments from the Seditionaries shop. Collages of the Continuous Monument and the Supersurface: a structure that covers the planet.
layers.gesture: Rigid, frontal posture, clothes that restrain and signal. The body is marked and bound. In Superstudio's drawings, it disappears into an infinite grid.
layers.decomposition: The provocation is absorbed by the market: the tear becomes a reproducible aesthetic and the radical collages end up in museums.

to_verify: Shop and Superstudio dates checked. Still to verify: which garment to show (the shop has no single piece) and the reading 'against linear progress' (Tafuri judged it self-advertising).

title: Portable Solitude & Black Japan

fashion.designer: Rei Kawakubo / Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto

design.artifact: Walkman TPS-L2, Japan, 1 July 1979 (US release June 1980)

layers.tension: Private intimacy in public space: individual listening and total black as a refusal of other people's gaze.
layers.material: Plastic and metal of the cassette player. Black wool and cotton, cuts and holes left in the fabric.
layers.artifacts: Sony TPS-L2: 33,000 yen, with two headphone sockets so two people could listen. Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto in Paris from 1981; the 'Holes' collection is from 1982-83.
layers.gesture: Walking with headphones on, unaware of those around you; dressing in black, asymmetric layers that hide the silhouette.
layers.decomposition: What seemed rude becomes normal: isolated listening no longer shocks. The hole in the fabric, born as a shock, becomes a reproducible style.

to_verify: The name 'Hiroshima chic' used by the press in 1981 needs a source (none found). The Walkman–Kawakubo pairing is our own reading, not a historical link.

title: Suburban Hyper-Consumerism & Memphis

fashion.artifact: Moncler puffer jacket, uniform of the Milanese paninari

layers.tension: Consumer boom and brand culture. Identity is bought, and youth groups recognise each other through labels and colours.
layers.material: Glossy nylon padded with down, decorated plastic laminate, graphic-pattern surfaces. Cheap material becomes decoration.
layers.artifacts: Moncler puffer jacket, worn by young Italian paninari. Sottsass's Carlton bookcase for the Memphis group, born in Milan.
layers.gesture: The body swells and shelters under the volume of the garment. The bookcase is a coloured totem more than a container.
layers.decomposition: The colour fades and the padding flattens. The brand survives as status, and Memphis design goes from scandal to collectable classic.

to_verify: Memphis (founded 6 December 1980, dissolved 1987) and Carlton (1981) checked. No source yet on the exact moment the Moncler jacket becomes a paninari symbol.

title: Darkwave / Industrial Cryptography

fashion.artifact: First collection, spring-summer 1989, Café de la Gare, Paris; Tabi shoe from 1989

design.artifact: Juicy Salif for Alessi: sketched in 1988, in production from 1990

layers.tension: Anonymity against the cult of the label: erasing the name and showing the construction, while design becomes a media icon.
layers.material: Raw cotton, a white label sewn with four visible stitches, cast aluminium and satin finishes that hide the author.
layers.artifacts: Garments and Tabi shoes by Maison Martin Margiela. Starck's Juicy Salif squeezer: a three-legged structure that looks like an insect.
layers.gesture: Face covered, body without a name: the gesture is to disappear. The object stands like a creature on the table rather than a tool.
layers.decomposition: Anonymity itself becomes a recognisable brand. The sculpture-object stops working and is displayed instead of used.

to_verify: Dates checked. The Margiela–Starck pair is a contrast (anonymity against star designer), not a direct link with darkwave: confirm this reading or change the object. The year of the white label is not documented in the sources found.

title: Tactical Cyberpunk

design.designer: Apple / Jonathan Ive and his team
design.artifact: iMac G3: announced 6 May 1998, on sale from August 1998

layers.tension: Surveillance, pollution and the network. Clothing becomes urban armour, while the computer enters the home as a colourful, friendly object.
layers.material: Technical nylon, padding, hoods and anti-smog masks. Coloured translucent polycarbonate for the computer's shell.
layers.artifacts: Vexed Generation outerwear with a high collar and hood. The iMac G3 in Bondi Blue: electronics that show their insides through the plastic.
layers.gesture: Closed posture, half-covered face, quick movement through the city. In front of the screen the body sits and looks inside.
layers.decomposition: The polycarbonate yellows and scratches. The tactical future becomes costume, and the colourful computer becomes a collector's piece.

to_verify: Vexed's founding in 1994 (from Wikipedia; another source says only 'mid-1990s'). The exact garments to show (parka, mask) are not confirmed by the sources. The phrase 'padding against police charges' comes from a source, not from us.

title: Y2K Utopianism & Liquid Digital

design.artifact: First-generation iPod: announced 23 October 2001, on sale from 10 November

layers.tension: Digital optimism at the end of the millennium and fear of computer collapse. Everything becomes liquid, glossy and portable.
layers.material: Grey slipcovers, wood, white plastic, polished steel. Surfaces that reflect and surfaces of the home.
layers.artifacts: Chalayan's Afterwords: a living room on the runway, chair covers become dresses and the table becomes a rigid skirt. First-generation iPod: 5 GB, 1,000 songs, 399 dollars, scroll wheel and steel back.
layers.gesture: The body evacuates carrying the home on itself; the thumb slides on the wheel, the headphones are white. Listening on the move, isolated in the city.
layers.decomposition: The gloss scratches and the battery dies. The format disappears with streaming, and the aesthetic returns as nostalgia.

to_verify: Rabanne has moved to specimen 002 (1960s). Still to decide whether Chalayan (2000) represents digital optimism well: the collection is about displacement and war. The period runs to 2005, beyond the 2000 of the title.
